content: 1. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, chest X-rays can be utilized as a screening tool for tuberculosis (TB) disease. This recommendation is conditional and based on moderate certainty of evidence regarding test accuracy. 2. For individuals aged 15 years and older in populations where TB screening is recommended, computer-aided detection (CAD) software programs may replace human readers for interpreting digital chest X-rays during TB screening and triage. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 3. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) may be used to screen for TB disease among adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation supported by moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 4. Early detection and treatment of TB in people living with HIV are critical to reducing morbidity and mortality. TB screening tools aim to identify individuals with a higher likelihood of TB disease, distinguishing them from those with a lower probability. Screening tests must be followed by diagnostic tests as part of a comprehensive clinical evaluation to confirm or rule out TB disease. 5. WHO recommends systematic TB screening for people living with HIV at every visit to a healthcare facility. This recommendation applies to all age groups and was first introduced in 2011. It remains in place to ensure early diagnosis and treatment, particularly in this high-risk group. 6. The WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS) has been evaluated for its diagnostic accuracy in detecting pulmonary TB among people living with HIV. The sensitivity of the W4SS is 83%, while its specificity is 38%. However, its utility is limited in certain subpopulations, such as outpatients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and pregnant women, due to lower sensitivity and specificity. 7. C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of general inflammation, can be measured using point-of-care tests on capillary blood. CRP has been shown to have similar or superior accuracy compared to the W4SS for TB screening when using a cut-off value of >5 mg/L. Combining CRP with the W4SS in parallel improves sensitivity and specificity for TB screening. 8. Chest X-rays (CXR) are recommended by WHO as an additional screening tool alongside the W4SS to rule out TB disease before initiating TB preventive therapy (TPT) in people living with HIV on ART. CXRs have similar sensitivity and higher specificity compared to the W4SS alone. The use of CXRs depends on the availability of radiological expertise and resources. 9. Computer-aided detection (CAD) software for interpreting digital chest X-rays offers a potential solution to the challenges of human interpretation, such as variability and limited availability of trained personnel. CAD software has been found to perform comparably to human readers in detecting TB-related abnormalities. WHO recommends CAD software for TB screening in settings where it has been externally validated. 10. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs), such as the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, are conditionally recommended for TB screening among adults and adolescents living with HIV in settings where TB prevalence exceeds 10%. These tests offer high sensitivity but may face challenges related to cost, access, and feasibility. 11. For medical inpatients living with HIV, WHO strongly recommends the use of mWRDs for rapid TB screening and diagnosis, regardless of symptoms. This recommendation is based on the high mortality risk in this population and the limited utility of the W4SS in such settings.
